newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal bank group stock in turmoil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal bank group stock in turmoil.

text.p: Top management changes in one of Portugal's leading bank groups -- Banco Totta and Banco Pinto & Sotto Mayor -- and surprising 1996 results, sent their stocks hurtling off in different directions on Monday.
Banco Totta & Acores crashed over 10 percent in heavy trade after announcing on Friday night that it would pay out far less than investors had been expecting in dividends on its 1996 results.
Sister bank Banco Pinto took off in the other direction, soaring over eight percent after the Friday announcement pledged a higher payout than had been predicted.
The turmoil on the Lisbon bourse, with Banco Pinto stock being suspended at one point, led the chairman of the Champalimaud group which controls both banks to issue a call for calm.

Antonio Champalimaud, whose son Luis was named chairman of both banks in the reshuffle on Friday, said that there was no reason for Totta to fall so sharply. He warned investors who sold that they risked losing money.
"This (drop in BTA share price) is too much and is not in any way justified. There is no reason for this," Champalimaud told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The veteran businessman, who rebuilt his fortune from scratch after the 1974 revolution, said that he personally would be demanding that the bank increase "significantly" the level of dividend that it was proposing to pay.
Banco Totta, whose former chairman Alipio Dias resigned on Friday, said that it would pay 135 escudos per share after its net profit fell 13 percent to 15 billion escudos ($93 million).
The bank had been expected to pay around 190 escudos, in line with the 1995 payout.
Banco Pinto, on the other hand, boosted profit 50 percent last year to 11.5 billion escudos. It said that it would hold the dividend unchanged at 60 escudos.
Champalimaud also dismissed any notion that the two banks might be merged in the foreseeable future.
The possibility of a merger had been another factor weakening Banco Totta, which is controlled by the Champalimaud group through Banco Pinto, because investors feared it could disappear.
"This (a fusion) is a very long process and it will only happen, in time, if there were an absolutely clear demonstration that it was wanted by all shareholders," he said.
"There is nothing to show, at the moment, that that is the case," he added.
